QF.id: Terminology in Equity and Debt Markets_32

question.text: Credit spread on a corporate bond refers to:

answer.text: The difference in coupon rate between two corporate bonds
The additional yield a corporate bond offers over a comparable government bond to compensate for credit risk
The difference between the bid and ask price
The spread between the repo rate and the bank rate

explanation.text: The Logic: A government bond of a given maturity is taken as the benchmark "risk-free" reference. Any corporate bond of comparable maturity will typically yield more than the government benchmark because investors demand compensation for the issuer's credit risk — the possibility of default or rating downgrade. That additional yield, expressed as the corporate yield minus the comparable government yield, is what the market calls the credit spread. Wider spreads imply higher perceived credit risk; narrower spreads imply better perceived credit quality or stronger investor appetite for the issuer. The Trap: The coupon-rate difference between two corporate bonds is just a coupon comparison, not a credit spread (which is a yield concept against a sovereign benchmark). The bid-ask spread is a liquidity/market-microstructure concept. The spread between the repo rate and the bank rate is an RBI policy-rate corridor, unrelated to corporate-bond credit risk. Note: The credit-spread definition as the additional corporate-bond yield over a comparable government bond is not stated on the cited NISM Series XV Research Analyst pages checked (pp.65-73, 234-235); those pages discuss default risk and bond pricing but not this specific definition. The framing above reflects general industry/regulatory usage of the term rather than the cited workbook chapter.
